prompt: A survey finds that adults who take a daily vitamin get fewer colds than adults who do not. The vitamin-takers also exercise much more. Why can we NOT conclude the vitamin prevents colds?

choices.label: Exercise is a confounding variable: it is mixed up with vitamin use and could be the real reason for fewer colds
The vitamin-takers had a placebo effect

hint: Two things differ between the groups, not one. Which other difference could explain fewer colds?

hints.text: Two things differ between the groups, not one. Which other difference could explain fewer colds?
The vitamin group also exercises more. If exercise reduces colds, you cannot tell whether the vitamin did anything.
Exercise is confounded with vitamin use: choice A.

explanation: The vitamin-takers and non-takers differ in TWO ways: vitamins and exercise.
Because exercise could reduce colds on its own, its effect is tangled with the vitamin's effect. That tangling is confounding.
Only a randomized experiment, which balances exercise across the groups, could separate the two. Choice A.

alternativeExplanations.title: What confounding means
steps: A confounding variable is associated with the explanatory variable AND affects the response.
Exercise is tied to vitamin use (same people) and plausibly affects colds.
That is the textbook definition, so exercise confounds the comparison.
